facts.statement: The genus Dinornis was described by Richard Owen in 1843.
facts.quote: authority: Owen, 1843

facts.statement: Dinornis fossils date from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Pleistocene-Holocene

facts.statement: All species of Dinornis went extinct by the year 1500.
facts.quote: extinct: 1500

facts.statement: Dinornis was endemic to New Zealand.
facts.quote: It was endemic to New Zealand.

facts.statement: Two valid species of Dinornis are the North Island giant moa and the South Island giant moa.
facts.quote: Two species of Dinornis are considered valid, the North Island giant moa (Dinornis novaezealandiae) and the South Island giant moa (Dinornis robustus).

facts.statement: Female Dinornis may have been the tallest bird ever, reaching approximately 3.6 meters in height.
facts.quote: Dinornis may have been the tallest bird that ever lived, with the females standing around 3.6 m tall

facts.statement: Female Dinornis are estimated to have weighed between 230 and 278 kilograms.
facts.quote: weighing an estimated 230 - 240 kg or 278 kg in various estimates

facts.statement: Male Dinornis were much smaller than females, weighing between 34 and 85 kilograms.
facts.quote: However, the males of the genus were much smaller, only around 34-85 kg.

facts.statement: Dinornis had reddish-brown, hair-like feathers covering most of its body.
facts.quote: Feather remains are reddish brown and hair-like

facts.statement: Dinornis had long necks and broad, sharp beaks adapted for eating vegetation from subalpine herbs to tree branches.
facts.quote: The birds had long, strong necks and broad sharp beaks that would have allowed them to eat vegetation from subalpine herbs through to tree branches.

facts.statement: Dinornis had large, powerful feet capable of delivering a strong kick when threatened.
facts.quote: The feet were large and powerful, and could probably deliver a powerful kick if threatened.

facts.statement: Dinornis eggs were enormous, roughly the size of a rugby ball and 80 times the volume of a chicken egg.
facts.quote: Dinornis eggs were enormous, as large as a rugby ball, and around 80 times the volume of a chicken's egg.

facts.statement: Male Dinornis likely incubated eggs for up to three months before hatching.
facts.quote: the male would have incubated the egg for up to three months before it hatched.

facts.statement: Giant moa chicks were able to see, run, and feed themselves immediately after hatching.
facts.quote: as soon as giant moa chicks hatched they would have been able to see, run and feed themselves.

facts.statement: Before humans arrived, Dinornis maintained a stable population in New Zealand for at least 40,000 years.
facts.quote: Prior to the arrival of humans, the giant moa had an ecologically stable population in New Zealand for at least 40,000 years.

facts.statement: Dinornis was wiped out by Polynesian settlers who hunted them for food.
facts.quote: The giant moa, along with other moa genera, were wiped out by Polynesian settlers, who hunted it for food.

facts.statement: Some sources estimate Dinornis could reach 3.7 meters in height and weigh 280 kilograms.
facts.quote: Se conocen dos especies, llamadas coloquialmente moas gigantes, las cuales llegaban a medir 3,7 m de altura y a tener un peso de 280 kg.

facts.statement: Dinornis had large, powerful feet and a long neck that allowed it to reach high vegetation.
facts.quote: Los pies eran grandes y poderosos, y tenían un cuello largo que les permitía llegar a la vegetación más alta.

facts.statement: Before human arrival, Dinornis had an ecologically stable population in New Zealand for at least 40,000 years.
facts.quote: Antes de la llegada de los humanos, esta ave había tenido una población ecológicamente estable en (lo que hoy se conoce como) Nueva Zelanda durante al menos 40.000 años.

facts.statement: Māori are known to have hunted Dinornis by driving them into holes and stealing their nests.
facts.quote: Se sabe que los maoríes todavía los cazaban a principios del , llevándolos a hoyos y robando a sus nidos.

facts.statement: The time range for Dinornis is from 0.129 million years ago to the present (Holocene).
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)
